topic: Day 2 · Haemostasis in Lower GI Bleeding — Endoscopic, Radiologic & Surgical
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Colorectal Surgery & GI Bleed MDT
speakerBio: Colorectal surgeon who chairs the emergency GI bleed MDT and has a one-rule philosophy she repeats to every trainee before theatre: localise before you cut, and never over-embolise a colon you want to keep alive.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

The CT angiogram is up on the screen: a bright blush of contrast pooling in the sigmoid. The 72-year-old man on the trolley has now had four units of red cells and is still bleeding. In the room are the endoscopist, the interventional radiologist, and the on-call surgeon, and the question is not whether to stop the bleed but how — and in what order. This session is the therapeutic climax of the lower GI bleeding pathway: the escalation ladder from colonoscopic haemostasis, to super-selective embolisation, to surgery as the last resort. The through-line is a single rule that separates a good outcome from a catastrophe: localise before you cut, and never over-embolise.

1 · 🪜 The escalation ladder — the mental model

Haemostasis in LGIB is a staged escalation, least invasive first, each rung reserved for failure of the last:

  1. Endoscopic (colonoscopic) therapy — first-line when a source is seen at colonoscopy in the stable patient.
  2. Radiologic — super-selective mesenteric embolisation — for ongoing bleeding localised on CTA/angiography, or when endoscopy fails or is unsafe.
  3. Surgery — the last resort, for uncontrolled bleeding after endoscopic and radiologic options are exhausted — and only, wherever possible, once the bleeding site is localised.
Endoscopy, then embolisation, then surgery — and localisation is the ticket that must be punched before the knife.
🎯 Multidisciplinary from the outset

The best outcomes come from a joint decision between gastroenterology, interventional radiology, and surgery — ideally activated early, not sequentially after each fails. The unstable, actively bleeding patient should be discussed by all three at once so the fastest route to definitive haemostasis is chosen, not defaulted to whoever answered the phone.

2 · 🔬 Colonoscopic therapy — the first-line tools

When colonoscopy identifies a bleeding lesion (active bleeding, a non-bleeding visible vessel, or an adherent clot), several endoscopic haemostatic modalities are available, often in combination:

ModalityHow it worksBest for
Through-the-scope clipsMechanical closure of the vessel/defectDiverticular bleed, post-polypectomy bleed, visible vessel
Thermal — bipolar/contact coagulation, heater probeCoagulates the vessel by heat + tamponadeVisible vessel, angiodysplasia (with argon plasma coagulation)
Argon plasma coagulation (APC)Non-contact thermal energy to a broad surfaceAngiodysplasia, radiation proctitis (superficial, multiple lesions)
Adrenaline (epinephrine) injectionVasoconstriction + tamponade — temporaryAdjunct only — buys a clear field; never sole therapy
Endoscopic band ligationRubber band strangles the vessel/lesionDiverticular bleeding, internal haemorrhoids, some post-polypectomy
Over-the-scope clipLarger, full-thickness mechanical graspRefractory or larger-vessel bleeds
⚠️ Adrenaline injection is never a standalone treatment

Dilute adrenaline (e.g. 1:10,000) achieves haemostasis by vasoconstriction and volume tamponade, but its effect is temporary and rebleeding is common once it wears off. It must always be combined with a definitive second modality — a clip or thermal coagulation. Using adrenaline alone and declaring victory is a classic set-up for rebleeding a few hours later.

3 · 🩸 Diverticular-specific endoscopic approaches

Diverticular bleeding poses a particular technical challenge — the culprit vessel sits at the neck or dome of a diverticulum, sometimes deep in the sac. Approaches:

  • Through-the-scope clips — direct clip of a visible vessel at the diverticular neck/dome, or clipping the diverticulum closed.
  • Endoscopic band ligation — suck the diverticulum into a cap and deploy a band over its base; increasingly favoured as effective and durable for diverticular bleeds.
  • Thermal coagulation — used cautiously; the thin colonic wall at a diverticulum raises perforation risk.
  • Adrenaline injection as an adjunct to gain a clear field before mechanical therapy.
💡 Find the stigma, treat the stigma

Definitive endoscopic therapy depends on identifying stigmata of recent haemorrhage — active bleeding, a non-bleeding visible vessel, or an adherent clot — at a specific diverticulum. A clean-based diverticulum with no stigmata does not need (and cannot usefully receive) targeted therapy. Careful washing and inspection to find the stigma is half the battle.

4 · 🎯 Super-selective mesenteric embolisation

When bleeding is ongoing and localised (usually on CTA, then confirmed at catheter angiography), the interventional radiologist can occlude the culprit vessel. The word that matters is super-selective: the catheter is advanced as distally as possible — to the vasa recta or marginal artery feeding the bleed — before deploying the embolic agent (microcoils, gelfoam, or PVA/microspheres).

  • Indications: ongoing bleeding localised on imaging; endoscopy failed, not feasible, or the patient too unstable to prep; a positive CTA blush.
  • Effectiveness: high immediate technical success in stopping the bleed.
  • The cardinal risk — bowel ischaemia from over-embolisation.
⚠️ Over-embolisation infarcts the colon

The colon has a relatively sparse collateral supply compared with the small bowel, so occluding a vessel too proximally — or embolising too large a territory — risks bowel ischaemia, infarction, and perforation. This is why the technique must be super-selective: occlude only the tiny distal branch feeding the bleeding point, preserving collateral flow to the surrounding bowel. The art is stopping the bleed while leaving the colon alive. Post-embolisation, watch for pain, fever, rising lactate, and signs of ischaemic complication.

5 · 🔪 Surgery — the last resort, and why localisation is everything

Surgery is reserved for the patient who is exsanguinating despite, or unsuitable for, endoscopic and radiologic haemostasis. The single most important determinant of a safe operation is whether the bleed has been localised.

Localised segmental resectionBlind subtotal colectomy
PrerequisiteBleeding site identified (endoscopy/CTA/angiography/scintigraphy)Source NOT localised — surgeon removes most of the colon empirically
OperationRemove the culprit segment onlyRemove colon caecum-to-rectum blindly
Rebleeding riskLow — the source is goneSignificant if the source was outside the resected field (e.g. small bowel)
Morbidity / mortalityLowerHigh — larger resection, sicker patient, worse physiology
Functional resultPreservedPoor — diarrhoea, stoma, major insult
💡 The rule that saves colons

Localise before you cut. A targeted segmental resection is a good operation; a blind subtotal colectomy for an unlocalised bleed is a dangerous one — high morbidity and mortality, and it still fails if the true source (say a small-bowel angiodysplasia) lies outside the resected colon. Every effort at localisation (repeat CTA, scintigraphy, on-table enteroscopy) is worth it to avoid operating blind.

6 · 📋 Master table — modality → indication → risk

ModalityPrimary indicationKey risk
Clips (TTS/OTS)Visible vessel, diverticular, post-polypectomyFailure to grasp deep vessel; rebleed
Thermal / APCVisible vessel; angiodysplasia, radiation proctitisPerforation (thin colonic wall), transmural injury
Adrenaline injectionAdjunct to gain a clear fieldTemporary only — rebleed if used alone
Band ligationDiverticular bleed, internal haemorrhoidsPerforation if full-thickness in thin-walled colon
Super-selective embolisationOngoing localised bleeding; endoscopy failed/unsafeBowel ischaemia/infarction from over-embolisation
Segmental resectionUncontrolled bleeding, source localisedAnastomotic leak; general surgical morbidity
Subtotal colectomy (blind)Exsanguinating, source NOT localised (avoid if possible)High morbidity/mortality; rebleed if source outside colon

7 · 🧭 Putting it together — the escalation in practice

  1. Stable, source seen at colonoscopy: treat endoscopically — clip/band/thermal ± adrenaline adjunct. Definitive and minimally invasive.
  2. Ongoing bleed, localised on CTA, endoscopy failed or unsafe: super-selective embolisation — stop the bleed, preserve the bowel.
  3. Uncontrolled despite the above, source localised: targeted segmental resection with the surgical team.
  4. Exsanguinating, source not localised: every effort to localise on the table (enteroscopy, re-look); blind subtotal colectomy only as a genuine life-saving last resort, with the patient and family aware of its heavy toll.
☠️ M&M — the blind colectomy for a bleed that was never localised

An 80-year-old man had recurrent brisk haematochezia. A first colonoscopy was unprepped and non-diagnostic; a CT angiogram, done after the bleeding had transiently stopped, was negative; no red-cell scintigraphy was arranged. Still bleeding and increasingly unstable, he was taken to theatre where — with no localisation — the surgeon performed a blind subtotal colectomy. He survived the operation but rebled from an ileal angiodysplasia within 48 hours (the source had never been in the colon), then died of multi-organ failure after a second laparotomy. Lessons: (1) the CTA should have been repeated while actively bleeding, and red-cell scintigraphy (most sensitive, catches intermittent bleeds) should have been used before resorting to surgery; (2) a blind colectomy removes the colon but not a small-bowel source — it carries high mortality and still fails if the bleed is extracolonic; (3) localise before you cut — on-table enteroscopy or provocative angiography were options; (4) the decision should have been a genuine MDT one, escalating the localisation effort rather than the size of the resection. The team escalated the operation instead of the diagnosis, and removed the wrong organ.

8 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Haemostasis escalates: colonoscopic therapy → super-selective embolisation → surgery, least invasive first, each rung for failure of the last.
  2. Colonoscopic tools: clips, thermal/APC, band ligation, with adrenaline only as an adjunct — never as sole therapy (it rebleeds).
  3. Diverticular bleeds are treated by clipping the visible vessel/neck or band ligation; find the stigma of recent haemorrhage first.
  4. Super-selective embolisation stops ongoing localised bleeding when endoscopy fails or isn't feasible — but over-embolisation infarcts the colon; occlude only the distal culprit branch.
  5. Surgery is the last resort: a targeted segmental resection is safe; a blind subtotal colectomy is dangerous, high-mortality, and fails if the source lies outside the colon.
  6. Localise before you cut, and make the decision multidisciplinary — gastroenterology, interventional radiology, and surgery together, early.

moderatorQs.q: Walk me through the escalation ladder for haemostasis in lower GI bleeding and what triggers moving up each rung.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: It is a staged escalation, least invasive first. Rung one is colonoscopic therapy — when a source is seen in the stable, prepped patient: clips, thermal coagulation or APC, band ligation, with adrenaline only as an adjunct. You move up when endoscopy fails, isn't feasible, or the patient is too unstable to prep. Rung two is super-selective mesenteric embolisation — for ongoing bleeding localised on CTA/angiography; you move up again if it fails or the bleed can't be reached. Rung three is surgery, the last resort for uncontrolled bleeding — ideally a targeted segmental resection once the source is localised. The triggers are ongoing bleeding plus failure or unsuitability of the current rung, and the whole ladder should be run as an early multidisciplinary decision, not sequential solo attempts.

moderatorQs.q: What is the principal danger of mesenteric embolisation, and how is it mitigated?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The principal danger is bowel ischaemia and infarction from over-embolisation. The colon has a comparatively sparse collateral supply, so occluding a vessel too proximally or embolising too large a territory can devascularise a segment of bowel, causing ischaemia, infarction, and perforation. It is mitigated by the super-selective technique: advancing the microcatheter as distally as possible — to the vasa recta or marginal artery feeding the exact bleeding point — before deploying microcoils, gelfoam, or particles, so that only the tiny culprit branch is occluded and collateral flow to surrounding bowel is preserved. Afterwards you monitor for ischaemic complications — increasing abdominal pain, fever, rising lactate — so that any infarcted segment is recognised early. The goal is to stop the bleed while keeping the colon alive.

moderatorQs.q: Why is a blind subtotal colectomy so dangerous, and what must happen before surgery for a lower GI bleed?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: A blind subtotal colectomy — removing the colon empirically when the bleeding source has not been localised — is dangerous for three reasons: it is a large resection in a physiologically compromised, actively bleeding patient, carrying high morbidity and mortality; it leaves the patient with a poor functional result; and, most treacherously, it still fails if the true source lies outside the colon (e.g. a small-bowel angiodysplasia or Meckel's), leading to continued or recurrent bleeding after a massive operation. What must happen first is localisation: exhaust colonoscopy, CT angiography while actively bleeding, red-cell scintigraphy, and small-bowel evaluation, and consider on-table enteroscopy. With a localised source, a targeted segmental resection is a far safer, lower-morbidity operation. The rule is simple — localise before you cut — and the decision should be made jointly with gastroenterology and interventional radiology.

audienceQs.q: Why can't we just inject adrenaline to stop a bleeding vessel at colonoscopy and be done?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because adrenaline (epinephrine) injection only buys you time, not a cure. It works by vasoconstriction and volume tamponade, which slows or stops the bleeding transiently and clears your field — but as the effect wears off, the vessel commonly rebleeds. So it must always be paired with a definitive second modality that mechanically or thermally seals the vessel: a through-the-scope clip, thermal/contact coagulation, or band ligation. Think of adrenaline as the tool that gives you a clean, dry view so you can place the clip accurately — never as the final treatment. Declaring haemostasis after adrenaline alone is a classic reason patients rebleed a few hours later.

audienceQs.q: For a diverticular bleed localised on CTA, how distal do I really need to be with the embolisation?
audienceQs.answerHTML: As distal as you can safely get — ideally to the vasa recta or the marginal artery branch directly feeding the bleeding point, rather than a proximal mesenteric trunk. The colon's collateral supply is relatively sparse, so a proximal occlusion risks ischaemia of a whole segment, whereas a truly super-selective occlusion of the single culprit branch stops the bleed while preserving surrounding perfusion. Practically that means advancing the microcatheter through the SMA/IMA into the terminal feeding vessel before deploying microcoils or gelfoam, and confirming the blush has stopped without sacrificing the marginal arcade. Then flag the team to watch for post-embolisation ischaemia — pain out of proportion, fever, rising lactate. Getting distal is the whole safety margin of the procedure.

audienceQs.q: The patient is crashing and we still don't have a precise source. Do I do a subtotal colectomy?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Only as a genuine, last-ditch life-saving measure — and push hard on localisation first, even intraoperatively. A blind subtotal colectomy in an unstable patient carries high morbidity and mortality and, critically, will not stop the bleeding if the source is in the small bowel (angiodysplasia, Meckel's) or was mis-attributed. So before or during the operation, use every rapid localisation option: a repeat CT angiogram if there's any window, and on-table enteroscopy or endoscopy to inspect small bowel and colon. If any segment is implicated, a targeted segmental resection is far safer. If the patient is truly exsanguinating with no localisation despite maximal effort, subtotal colectomy may be unavoidable — but it is a rescue of last resort made jointly with the MDT, with eyes open to its failure rate, not a default for a bleed nobody bothered to localise.
